nameStory: The horned lark gets its name from the distinctive black feather tufts that stick up like tiny horns from the male's head during breeding season. These 'horns' are actually specialized feathers that can be raised or lowered, making the bird look almost devilish when alert. In Europe, the same species is called the 'shore lark' because flocks gather along coastlines during winter months.
description: The horned lark is a ground-dwelling songbird about the size of a sparrow, measuring 6-8 inches long. Males in breeding plumage sport a striking yellow face with bold black markings and those famous horn-like feather tufts on their heads. The back is brown and streaky for camouflage, while the underparts are pale. Females and non-breeding males are more subdued but still show the distinctive facial pattern, just less boldly marked.

idTips.label: Horn tufts
idTips.description: Males display small black feather tufts that project upward from behind their eyes like tiny horns - most visible when the bird is alert or excited

idTips.label: Yellow face pattern
idTips.description: Bright yellow face with bold black markings forming a distinctive mask around the eyes and across the forehead, though duller in females and winter birds

idTips.label: Ground behavior
idTips.description: Walks and runs along the ground rather than hopping, often crouching low with a horizontal posture when foraging

idTips.label: Tinkling flight call
idTips.description: Makes soft, high-pitched 'tseee-titi' or tinkling notes when flying overhead in loose flocks, especially during migration

idTips.label: Black breast band
idTips.description: Shows a distinctive black band or bib across the upper chest that contrasts with the pale belly, most prominent in breeding males

habitat: Look for horned larks in wide-open spaces with short grass or bare ground - airports, large farm fields, golf courses, and coastal areas. They prefer sparse vegetation where they can easily walk and run while foraging for seeds and insects. During winter, they're often found in flocks on beaches, mudflats, and recently plowed agricultural fields.

seasonality.spring: Males arrive on breeding territories and develop their brightest plumage with prominent horn tufts and bold facial markings. Listen for their tinkling flight songs as they perform aerial displays.
seasonality.summer: Breeding birds are most easily identified with full horn tufts and bright yellow faces. Look for them walking through short grass areas, often with young following behind.
seasonality.fall: Flocks begin forming as birds move toward wintering areas. Horn tufts are less prominent and colors more muted, but facial patterns still visible.
seasonality.winter: Found in loose flocks on beaches and open fields, often mixed with other ground-feeding birds. Plumage is dullest now but still shows the basic yellow and black face pattern.

funFact: Horned larks are one of the few songbirds that regularly take dust baths - they'll find a patch of fine dirt or sand and vigorously flutter their wings while squatting down, coating their feathers with dust to help control parasites and keep their plumage in top condition.
confusionNotes: The distinctive yellow face with black markings separates horned larks from all other New England ground birds. Pipits might be found in similar habitat but lack the bold facial pattern and are more brown overall. Remember: if it has a yellow face with black 'horns' and walks on the ground, it's a horned lark.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'horned,' the tufts are actually specialized feathers, not true horns. This is the only true lark species that regularly occurs in New England - other birds called 'larks' like meadowlarks are actually in the blackbird family.
compareHints: The horned lark is the only member of the true lark family regularly found in New England, so there are no close relatives to compare. Among similar ground-dwelling birds, pipits are the closest in behavior but lack the horned lark's bold yellow and black facial pattern and have more subdued brown plumage overall. Horned larks also have a more upright posture when alert compared to pipits' more horizontal stance.
